---
title: "From object literals to classes"
---

Year one gave you two tools for building your own data: a `type` that names the
fields, and an object literal that fills them in. A function that works on such
an object takes it as a parameter. That carries you a long way, and it creaks
once six functions all belong to the same kind of object and nothing in the code
says so. A class says so. Type the small version and watch what moves.

::: {.callout-note}
## New part, new buddy code

Part 4 has its own coding buddy, and this one knows classes. Your teacher hands
out the code for it, and you put it into `~/.pi/agent/auth.json` in place of the
Part 3 code. The setup chapter in Part 1 shows that file.
:::

## Two counters, the year-one way {#sec-classes-literal}

1. Create a new app `counter-classes` from our template inside `coursework/`.
2. Replace everything in `src/index.ts` with this:

   ```ts
   type Counter = {
     count: number;
     step: number;
   };

   const increase = (counter: Counter): void => {
     counter.count += counter.step;
   };

   const clicks: Counter = { count: 0, step: 1 };
   const score: Counter = { count: 0, step: 10 };

   increase(clicks);
   increase(score);
   increase(score);

   console.log(clicks.count, score.count);
   ```

3. Run `npm start` and open the console with F12.

The console shows `1 20`. Two objects of the same shape, each with its own two
numbers, and one function that works on either of them. `increase(clicks)`
changes the real `clicks` because the object travels into the function as a
reference, the way year one described it.

Now look at the shape of the code instead of the result. The type sits in one
place and the function in another, and the only tie between them is the
parameter type of `increase`. Add `reset` and `decrease` and that tie gets
thinner with every function.

## The same two counters as a class {#sec-classes-class}

Replace everything in `src/index.ts` again:

```ts
class Counter {
  count: number;
  step: number;

  constructor(step: number) {
    this.count = 0;
    this.step = step;
  }

  increase(): void {
    this.count += this.step;
  }
}

const clicks = new Counter(1);
const score = new Counter(10);

clicks.increase();
score.increase();
score.increase();

console.log(clicks.count, score.count);
```

The console shows `1 20` again. Same two counters, same result, and the function
that changes them now lives inside the braces of the class. The call turned from
`increase(clicks)` into `clicks.increase()`, which is how you have been calling
`button.addEventListener` and `list.append` since Part 2.

## What the parts of a class are called {#sec-classes-parts}

A class is a blueprint. `class Counter { ... }` says what every counter has and
what every counter can do, and it holds no numbers of its own. Class names are
written in PascalCase, so `Counter` and never `counter`.

`count` and `step` are **fields**, the data each counter carries. Declare them
at the top with their types, and a reader knows after four lines what a counter
is made of. The **constructor** below them runs once for each new object and
puts the fields into a sensible starting state, here with `step` arriving as a
parameter and `count` starting at zero. `increase` is a **method**, a function
that belongs to the class, and methods come after the constructor.

`new Counter(10)` builds one object from the blueprint. It reserves a fresh
`count` and a fresh `step`, runs the constructor with `10`, and hands the
finished object back. Two calls to `new` give two objects that share nothing,
which is why `score.increase()` leaves `clicks` untouched.

`this` is the object the method was called on. In `clicks.increase()` the body
runs with `this` being `clicks`, and the same body runs with `this` being
`score` for the other counter. Delete that word once, so that `increase` reads
`count += this.step;`, and TypeScript answers:

```
error TS2663: Cannot find name 'count'. Did you mean the instance member 'this.count'?
```

Inside a method, a bare `count` means a variable of that method. A field needs
`this.` in front of it, every single time.

## You have been making objects from classes all year {#sec-classes-dom}

Add two lines at the end of `src/index.ts` and save:

```ts
const button = document.createElement('button');
console.log(button.constructor.name);
console.log(clicks.constructor.name);
```

The console prints `HTMLButtonElement` and `Counter`. Every object remembers the
class it was built from, and `constructor.name` asks it for that name, the same
way it told you `SVGCircleElement` back in Part 3.

`HTMLButtonElement` is a class the browser makers wrote. `disabled` is one of
its fields, `addEventListener` one of its methods, and
`document.createElement('button')` looks up that blueprint and runs its
constructor for you. Your program has been full of objects made from classes
since Part 2, and the only new part today is that the blueprint is yours.

## A type with exactly two values {#sec-classes-union}

Connect Four has two players. Storing the current one as a `string` lets
`'blue'` and `'ylelow'` through without a word from TypeScript. Write the
allowed values as the type instead:

```ts
type Player = 'red' | 'yellow';
type Cell = Player | 'empty';
```

The `|` is the same "one of these" bar you met in `HTMLElement | null` in Part 2,
this time between two fixed pieces of text. A variable of type `Player` holds
`'red'` or `'yellow'`, VS Code offers you both while you type, and a typo gets
caught:

```
error TS2322: Type '"blue"' is not assignable to type 'Player'.
```

`Cell` shows that a union can build on another union: a cell holds a player's
disc or the word `'empty'`. Other languages call such a small fixed set of
values an enum, and Part 4 comes back to that word later.

## A field can hold a whole board {#sec-classes-board}

A field is a variable that belongs to the object, so it can hold an array, and
an array of arrays:

```ts
class MiniBoard {
  cells: Cell[][] = [
    ['empty', 'empty', 'empty'],
    ['empty', 'empty', 'empty'],
  ];

  put(row: number, column: number, player: Player): void {
    const line = this.cells[row];
    if (line === undefined) {
      return;
    }
    line[column] = player;
  }
}
```

`cells` is a `Cell[][]`, an array of rows where each row is an array of cells,
which is the 2D array from year one with a much stricter type. A field whose
starting value is written right there needs no constructor.

The two lines around `line` are what `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` in your
`tsconfig.json` asks of you. `this.cells[row]` has the type
`Cell[] | undefined`, because TypeScript cannot know that `row` is inside the
array, so you check instead of reaching for `!`. Pull that check into one small
method and the rest of the class stays readable.

## Listeners and the `this` trap {#sec-classes-listener}

A class that draws a board also reacts to clicks, and the listener needs a way
back to the object:

```ts
cell.addEventListener('click', () => {
  this.dropDisc(column);
});
```

An arrow function has no `this` of its own. It borrows the `this` of the code
around it, which here is the method that created the listener, so the click
reaches your object. Hand `addEventListener` a plain function instead and the
browser calls it with `this` set to the clicked element, and a button has no
`dropDisc` on it. So the rule for the rest of this book is that a listener which
needs the object is written as an arrow function.

::: {.research title="Filling an array, and drawing a round disc"}
The board in the exercise is six rows of seven cells, and `Array.from` builds it
in one line as long as you know which one-liner is a trap. The discs are buttons
in a CSS Grid, and a button stays a flat rectangle until your stylesheet says
otherwise.

1. `Array.from({ length: 7 }, () => 'empty')` gives you an array. What is the
   second argument for, and what is in the array afterwards?
2. Compare `new Array(6).fill([])` with `Array.from({ length: 6 }, () => [])`.
   One of them gives six separate inner arrays, the other gives six names for
   one and the same array. Which is which, and what would the second one do to a
   game board?
3. Which CSS property turns a square box into a circle, and which one keeps a
   grid cell exactly as tall as it is wide without naming a pixel size?

Question 2 is exam material: the exam runs without internet and without AI next
to you.
:::

## Exercise: Connect Four {#sec-classes-exercise}

Two players drop discs into a board of seven columns and six rows, and a disc
falls to the lowest free cell of its column. Four discs of one color in a row, a
column, or a diagonal win the game, and a full board with no such line is a
draw. One class holds the board, the rules, and the buttons on screen.

{{< exercise connect-four >}}

The page is ready: an empty `<div id="board">`, an empty `<p id="status">`, and
a button `restartButton`. The stylesheet lays the board out as a grid of seven
columns on a blue background and paints a cell white, red, or yellow, and it
leaves one job to you that step 5 names. You write `src/index.ts` from nothing.

1. Delete both lines the template put into `src/index.ts` and start the file
   with `import './styles.css';`. Under it go the two types
   `type Player = 'red' | 'yellow';` and `type Cell = Player | 'empty';`, then
   the two constants `const ROWS = 6;` and `const COLUMNS = 7;`.
2. Open `class ConnectFourGame` and declare seven fields at the top, each with
   its type: `board: Cell[][]`, `cells: HTMLButtonElement[][]`,
   `currentPlayer: Player`, `gameOver: boolean`, `discCount: number`,
   `boardElement: HTMLDivElement`, and `statusElement: HTMLParagraphElement`.
   `board` is the game in memory and `cells` the game on screen, in the same row
   and column order.
3. Write the constructor, without parameters. Fetch `#board`, `#status`, and
   `#restartButton` with `querySelector<...>`, throw one error when any of the
   three is missing, and store the board and the status paragraph in their
   fields. Give `board` and `cells` an empty array, `currentPlayer` the value
   `'red'`, `gameOver` the value `false`, and `discCount` the value `0`.
4. Write the method `buildCells(): void`. Two nested loops over `ROWS` and
   `COLUMNS` create one `button` element per cell, set its `type` to `'button'`,
   add the class `cell` to it, and append it to `this.boardElement`. Collect the
   buttons of one row in an array and push that array into `this.cells`. Call
   `this.buildCells()` at the end of the constructor, and put
   `new ConnectFourGame();` as the last line of the file. No variable has to
   hold that object, because everything from here on happens in its listeners.
   Run `npm start`. Expected result: a thin blue bar, because all 42 buttons are
   in the grid with no height yet.
5. Give the cells their shape. Add two properties to the `.cell` rule in
   `src/styles.css`, one that rounds a box into a circle and one that keeps each
   cell as tall as it is wide. Expected result: 42 white discs in six rows of
   seven on a blue board, each one turning light blue under the mouse pointer.
6. Write `start(): void`, the method that begins a round. It fills `this.board`
   with `ROWS` rows of `COLUMNS` cells, all `'empty'`, using `Array.from`. Write
   the return type on both arrow functions, `Cell[]` outside and `Cell` inside,
   so the result is a `Cell[][]` and not an array of plain strings. Then set
   `currentPlayer` back to `'red'`, `gameOver` to `false`, and `discCount` to
   `0`, clear the classes `red` and `yellow` off every button in `this.cells`
   with two `for...of` loops, and put `Red starts.` into the status paragraph.
   Call `this.start()` as the last line of the constructor. Expected result: the
   line under the board reads `Red starts.`
7. Write two reading helpers. `cellAt(row: number, column: number): Cell` looks
   up `this.board[row]` and then the cell, and answers `'empty'` whenever one of
   the two is `undefined`. Answering `'empty'` for a place outside the board is
   a decision that pays off in step 10.
   `freeRowIn(column: number): number` walks from `ROWS - 1` up to `0` and
   returns the first row whose `cellAt` is `'empty'`, or `-1` for a full
   column.
8. Write three tiny helpers. `paintCell(row, column, player)` reaches the button
   through `this.cells`, checking for `undefined` the way `cellAt` does, and
   adds the player's word as a class to it. `switchPlayer()` flips
   `currentPlayer` between the two values. `nameOf(player: Player): string`
   returns `Red` or `Yellow` for the status line.
9. Write `dropDisc(column: number): void`. Return right away when
   `this.gameOver` is `true`. Ask `freeRowIn` for the row, and when it answers
   `-1`, put `That column is full. Pick another one.` into the status paragraph
   and return. Otherwise write `this.currentPlayer` into `this.board` at that
   place, call `paintCell` for the same place, and add one to `discCount`.
   Finish with `this.switchPlayer()` and a status line such as `Yellow is next.`
   Now wire the board up: in `buildCells`, give every button a `click` listener
   that is an arrow function calling `this.dropDisc(column)`. Expected result: a
   click anywhere in a column drops a disc onto its lowest free cell, and the
   colors alternate.
10. Find a winning line with three methods.
    `countInDirection(row, column, rowStep, columnStep, player)` starts one step
    away from the new disc and walks on while `cellAt` keeps answering with that
    player, counting as it goes. It needs no border check, because `cellAt`
    answers `'empty'` outside the board. `countLine` returns `1` plus that count
    plus the count in the opposite direction, which you get by passing
    `-rowStep` and `-columnStep`, so it measures the whole line through the new
    disc. `isWin(row, column, player)` returns `true` when `countLine` reaches 4
    or more in any of the directions `(0, 1)`, `(1, 0)`, `(1, 1)`, and
    `(1, -1)`. Those four cover all eight, because every line is measured both
    ways.
11. End the game. In `dropDisc`, right after counting the disc, ask `isWin`.
    When it says yes, set `gameOver` to `true`, put a line such as `Red wins!`
    into the status paragraph, and return. Otherwise, when `discCount` has
    reached `ROWS * COLUMNS`, set `gameOver` to `true`, write
    `The board is full. Nobody wins.`, and return. The player switches only
    after those two checks. Expected result: four in a row stops the game, and
    further clicks change nothing.
12. Make the restart button work. In the constructor, add a `click` listener to
    the restart button that calls `this.start()` from an arrow function.
    Expected result: the board empties, the status line says `Red starts.`, and
    a new game runs.
13. Run `npm run verify` and fix what it reports.

Two extras if you finish early. Switch the six buttons of a full column to
`disabled` instead of writing a message about it. Count the games each player
has won in two more fields and show both numbers next to the status line.

::: {.callout-note}
## What has to work

* The app starts with `npm start`, the console stays clean, and `npm run verify`
  passes.
* The board shows six rows of seven round cells, and a click drops a disc to the
  lowest free cell of its column.
* Four in a row horizontally, vertically, or diagonally ends the game and names
  the winner.
* The restart button starts a fresh game at any time.

Diagonal wins and the draw are what lift this above passing.
:::
